name: The Five Phases
title: The Five Phases
answer: The Five Phases is a staged method for bringing an AI tool into a school: assess readiness, choose the pilot, set up governance, run and evaluate, and scale what works. Each phase ends with a deliverable a leader can hold in their hand, and each has a named owner. The method exists to stop a promising tool from turning into an expensive disappointment through skipped steps.

sections.body: The Five Phases treats adoption as a sequence rather than a single decision, so that a school moves from judging its own readiness, to picking one pilot, to putting governance in place, to running and evaluating that pilot, and only then to scaling what worked. Each phase closes with a concrete deliverable and an assigned owner, which means progress can be seen and accounted for rather than assumed. The problem it solves is the common pattern in which a tool is bought or launched before anyone has checked readiness, set rules, or agreed how success will be judged. Skipping a phase is described as the most common route from a promising tool to an expensive disappointment. The phases are not meant to be slow by default, but they are meant to be complete.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The text does not divide the method by grade band. It divides it by stakes and by the size of the district. A small district can move through the first three phases in a month for a low risk tool such as a lesson planning assistant. A tool that touches student records, or that informs decisions about students, deserves more time at every step. The rule of thumb given is that the higher the stakes, the slower the phases should run.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers no study, figure or finding to support the method, and it carries no evidence label. Figure 4.2 is referenced as a list of each phase with its deliverable and owner, which is a planning aid rather than research. This idea therefore rests on practice and on the author's operating experience rather than on research evidence.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The main risk named in the text is skipping a phase, which is described as the most common way a promising tool becomes an expensive disappointment. The text also sets a limit on speed: the higher the stakes, the slower the phases, so tools touching student records or decisions about students are not to be rushed. Responsibility stays with people rather than with the tool, since every phase has a named owner and ends in a deliverable a leader can hold. The text does not set out further limits, and it does not address legal duties.
